findings.title: Batch is serialized after the buffer has already cleared it, so audit events are lost
findings.scenario: auditBatchSize is 2. recordAudit adds two events, so EventBuffer.add calls flush(), which calls write(this.items) and then sets this.items.length = 0. The write only queues the closure. Its events.map runs later, on the same array, which is now empty, so appendFile writes an empty string. findings.title: Lockout key uses the raw email, so case and whitespace variants get separate counters
findings.scenario: Sending 'Victim@Example.com', 'victim@example.com', ' victim@example.com ' and so on gives each variant its own 5-attempt window. findByEmail normalizes with trim and lowercase (src/emails.js:1), so every variant resolves to the same account, and the per-account limit can be bypassed by varying the casing. Each variant allows 5 guesses per 15 minutes, so the attacker's effective limit grows with the number of variants.

The diff adds no test that sends a second casing of the same email, and no test in the repo references login (Grep for 'login|attempts' matched only src/routes.js and src/login.js).

findings.title: Missing-account guard throws before the lock is released, so the retry hangs the worker
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber is picked up. The guard runs after acquire() but outside the try/finally, so it throws without calling release(). locks.js keeps payout:<id> in `held`. worker.js catches the error and calls job.retryLater(). The retry calls acquire('payout:<id>'), which loops on held.get(key).promise, and that promise never resolves. runPayouts awaits sendPayout one job at a time, so the whole worker stalls.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only release() call is in the finally block at line 18, and the guard sits before that try. Nothing in locks.js times out or expires held entries, and worker.js does not release locks on error.

findings.title: Signed event without data.shipmentId throws and the request never gets a response
findings.scenario: A validly signed body such as {"type":"in_transit"} (no data), or the literal body null, makes event.data.shipmentId or event.type throw a TypeError. handleShippingWebhook rejects, and the async request listener in src/server.js (line 6-15) has no catch, so the response is never ended and the rejection is unhandled. Node's default unhandled-rejection mode terminates the process.
findings.whyNotPrevented: server.js has no try/catch around the handler call at line 14, and webhooks.js only guards JSON.parse. The docs in src/shipping-events.js say data is absent only on ping, but nothing enforces that shape.

findings.title: Events for unknown shipments are acknowledged with 200 and dropped

findings.whyNotPrevented: updateShipment returns null for a missing id and the handler ignores the return value. Nothing in the diff creates the shipment or queues the event.

forbidden.title: Signed event without data.shipmentId crashes the server

findings.title: Signed event without data.shipmentId crashes the server
findings.scenario: A validly signed body such as {"type":"in_transit"} (no data field, which the provider's own typedef in shipping-events.js does not allow for non-ping events) makes event.data undefined, so the property read throws a TypeError. The throw escapes handleShippingWebhook, and in src/server.js line 14 the handler is awaited inside an async request listener with no catch. Node's default unhandled-rejection behavior then exits the process, and the request never gets a response.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No try/catch or shape check exists in src/webhooks.js or src/server.js. The signature check only proves the sender holds the secret, not that the payload matches the documented shape, and no test covers a malformed signed body.

findings.title: Signed payload without data crashes the process
findings.scenario: A correctly signed body such as {"type":"in_transit"} (no data) makes event.data undefined, so event.data.shipmentId throws. The body JSON "null" fails earlier at event.type on line 33. The async route handler in src/server.js (line 6 and line 14) has no catch and no process-level unhandledRejection handler (grep found none), so Node exits, and the request gets no response.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only guards are the signature check and the JSON.parse try/catch. Nothing checks the shape of event or event.data after parsing, and src/shipping-events.js documents data as required on every non-ping event, which the code does not enforce.

findings.title: Saved preferences leak into the shared defaults object and across users
findings.scenario: User A saves theme 'dark'. preferencesFor(A) writes into DEFAULT_PREFERENCES because defaultPreferences() returns that same object (src/defaults.js line 8), not a copy. A later request for user B, who has no saved preferences, returns theme 'dark' and any other keys A saved. The defaults also stay changed for the life of the process.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaults.js returns the module-level object by reference, and preferences.js mutates it without copying. No test covers two consecutive calls, so nothing catches the shared state.

findings.title: `in` check accepts inherited Object.prototype keys as supported preferences
findings.scenario: A saved key "constructor" or "toString" passes the check because `in` also searches the prototype chain. It is then written onto the result, so the response carries an unsupported key. A saved key "__proto__" set to an object would change the result's prototype.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check uses `in` instead of an own-property test such as Object.hasOwn, and no test covers unsupported keys.

findings.title: Saved preferences leak into the shared defaults and across users
findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself (src/defaults.js line 8: return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;). User A with savedPreferences {theme: 'dark'} makes preferencesFor() write theme='dark' into that shared object. findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() returns the same object on every call and nothing copies it. No test in the diff calls preferencesFor twice with different users.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The check only tests membership with `in`. Nothing filters inherited names.
